utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. I remind you that the solemn undertaking to tell the truth which you took yesterday at the start of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, I neglected yesterday to introduce a new face on our team. April Carter was sitting in with me yesterday and will be here assisting today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We talked about how you were hiding out in Gjakova town during the time of the NATO campaign. Before that bombing started in March of 1999, do you have a rough idea of how many people of all ethnicities lived in Gjakova town, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the statistics of 1981, which were the last official statistics, the population counted about 120.000. Now the population is 158.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know the number for the entire municipality of Gjakova, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- the figures I gave apply to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the town itself, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly 50 per cent of that population lives in the town, or maybe 45 per cent. The rest lives in rural areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of those numbers, do you know the approximate percentage of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanians make up the majority, not only in Gjakova but all over Kosova; whereas the Serbs, in politics they make up the majority. In terms of population, they account for about 2 per cent, not more than that; whereas the other minorities I think account for 0.2 per cent, very, very little figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So are you saying in Gjakova municipality the Albanians were more than 90 or 95 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have -- based on your work with the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms, did you have any idea how many Kosovo Albanians left the municipality during the first half of 1999?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you only approximate figures, which means that about 70 per cent of the population left for Albania. It is hard to give you an accurate figure, but this is an approximate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell the Court, do you have knowledge about what the atmosphere was among the Kosovo Albanians in Gjakova at the time of the NATO bombing and with regard to the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 24th, that is the first day of NATO air-strikes, the night of 24th of March, after midnight, the city started to burn. Until that time, over 55 villages were burned, either partially or completely. About 40.000 inhabitants had been driven out of their villages and found shelter in Gjakova because the villages were shelled by the Serb forces. A situation of terror prevailed. It was constant terror. That night, over 200 bars and restaurants were torched in the old town, and five persons were killed in the neighbourhood where I live. And the terror continued for 78 days and nights on end, until the coming of the NATO troops. So in answer to your first question, this is what I think about NATO. Hadn't it been for NATO, the Albanians would have been the most retched population living under that regime. So with NATO, the miracle happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before I lose track of this for the moment, in -- when you were asked about the proportion of the population that were Serbian you said that although they were a very small percentage, they occupied most of the political positions. And the answer has been translated as if that was the situation today. When you say that Serbs occupied most of the political positions, are you referring to 1999 or are you referring also to today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refer to that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this percentage applied to that time; now, it's non-existent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have to say -- I have to add that I meant the Serbs and Montenegrins because we had both of them living in Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in paragraph 45 of your statement, which is on page 8 of the English and page 9 at the top of the B/C/S, you refer to in April seeing what you described as a river of people leaving during that time. Where were these people coming from that you saw?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The long convoys of people, which started in early April 1999, were formed as a result of the scenario prepared by these forces to drive out the Albanians from our municipality and from the entire Kosova and to send them to Albania. They entered, the Serb forces entered Albanian houses, drove the inhabitants out through use of force, threatening them: Go out because you have asked for NATO to come. You ask for Albania. So go to Albania. That is your homeland. Kosova is a Serbian country. And under threat of arms and being insulted all the time, beaten and maltreated, brutally tortured, their IDs being torn up, sometimes being violated, they were forced to free [as interpreted] their own country on the pretext of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, to flee --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see in the -- [Previous translation continues] ... they were forced to free --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from what he said before that probably should read "flee." Is that correct, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, they were forced to flee, to leave?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were forced to flee the country, to flee the country because of force being exercised against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the next approximate paragraph you say that in late April you saw police coming around town registering the Albanians who were still in town. In late April, do you have an idea of how many Kosovo Albanians remained in the town of Gjakova?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not at the end of April but until the 13th of May. As I said earlier, about 70 per cent of the population were forced to leave their homes and go to Albania. Some of them were arrested and ended up in prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So do you know why this remaining 30 per cent were not being killed or were not being forced to leave to go to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on just now, please, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this calls for pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I disagree. I think as long as it's made clear, Mr. Hannis, to the witness that what we need to know is what he personally can tell us from his experience of being there and seeing and hearing what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my original question is, first: Do you know, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And depending on what his answer is, I'll have a question to follow up to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, let me ask again: Do you know why this remaining 30 per cent was allowed to remain and were not being killed or imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people here would know better. Probably to keep them hostages, to keep, let's say, a kind of balance, to use them later for their own purposes, which they must know better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- let me follow up then with pointing out --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To keep that part of population under control. It was easier for them to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think now I see forcing the point that Mr. Lukic is making. What I was expecting to hear was an answer based on knowledge from within the community, but clearly what this question is being interpreted by the witness is as seeking is his conclusions about the actions of those who were causing this in his view, and that's not appropriate, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was expecting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's made it clear he's not in a position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was expecting to see a yes or no and then asking him how he knew and what he based it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in your statement in paragraphs 24 to 28, which begin on page 6 of both the English and the B/C/S and paragraphs 32 to 44, which start on page 7, you provide some specific information about -- first of all, about six specific killings and then about some additional killings, looting, arson, and expulsions. What was the source of your information for those incidents that you describe in your statement? Was that first-hand knowledge? Knowledge from other sources? How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when these crimes were committed, it was the first night. That night I was hiding out in Blloku i Ri, as I said yesterday. But from my home they called me up and told me that these and this persons have been killed. I knew all of them because they lived in the same neighbourhood with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that refers to the first six killings you describe in paragraphs 24 through 28. In paragraphs 32 to 44 you talk about several different incidents throughout the municipality, including killings, lootings, arson and expulsions. What was the source of your information for those items? Was that again people who called you or was that work you did after the bombing was over?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. There is another objection taken to this. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have to object. Mr. Hannis is leading this witness through his direct testimony, and again this is not 92 bis. This is a witness who is testifying live who is being led -- who is being fed leading questions and asked to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's nothing leading about the question, what was the source of your information for these items, but it's the next part, I take it, that you're objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the whole question beginning on line 11. We've had several questions like this. He points to paragraphs in the statement. He says this, this, and this and that happened. You told us about that. Was it because of expulsion or violence or did someone tell you anything? I mean, these are just leading questions of a viva voce witness, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that general point can't be right, surely. If a witness has given evidence about a number of killings, there's nothing wrong with you then asking him what was the source of his information about these killings. But I agree with you that it's wrong then to say: Was that again people who called you or was that what you did after the bombing was over? Pointing in the direction of answers that would be acceptable for the Prosecution. I agree with that. But I think -- I'm not sympathetic to the general point that to use this as a sign-post in the way in this evidence is being presented is wrong. Now, Mr. Hannis, you've rather undermined the potential for a helpful answer, I think, in relation to the second section of items that you're talking about. Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, yesterday there was an objection to the way the pages were marked, so I would ask my learned friend to be more precise when giving us the page references. We don't have the important paragraphs he's referring to, so could we have at least the page number and the number of the paragraph being referred to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, that's yet another difficulty that arises because these statement -- this particular statement isn't numbered paragraphs. It would be helpful, I think, if statements could in future rather than be numbered by page could be numbered by paragraphs and hopefully translated according to these paragraph numbers. However, can you assist counsel from now on as far as possible with clearer identification of where the material is? I think we can see the six killings that are referred to fairly easily. They are listed as six deaths and then the material -- the circumstances are referred to and then you have moved on to the section after that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And paragraphs 32 to 44 begin -- paragraph 32 begins on page 7 of the B/C/S right below the second dotted line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, I'm sustaining the objection to the leading nature of the last question which you posed and invite you to approach this a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Mr. Hannis, we would not like the word "paragraph" to be used. This brings us into difficulties. This transcript will remain. When he says "paragraphs 22 to 24," where is that? That's something which he's looking at which doesn't exist anywhere else. I can follow by the content not the numbers, so please don't say "paragraph 22, 24," just give us the page number and say what line it is from the bottom. For example, now you are referring to line 246 from the bottom, and that will solve the problem. If you say "paragraph," when I look at the transcript tomorrow I don't have the paragraph number. You're using something that doesn't exist. The lines exist. Thank you. That's the only solution I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't think that -- thank you, Mr. Fila. I don't think there's a particular problem at the moment. The witness clearly understands what he's being asked about, and he's not looking at a statement to check paragraph numbers. So I think so far we've been able to identify the areas that matter, but I think the point is well that for future record purposes it may be important to identify the areas by page rather than paragraph number, except in future statements where perhaps we could have the paragraphs actually numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I wish someone had thought of that in 1999 and 2000 when many of these statements were taken. With regard to paragraph -- what I've referred to as paragraph 32, in the B/C/S that starts on page 7, ten lines up from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to those events that you've described, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, what was the source of your information? Was that stuff that you witnessed first-hand?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I have seen myself; some others witnesses have reported to us in the office. Sometimes I have gone myself to the site of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with witnesses, the last paragraph in your statement, page 9 of the B/C/S, you indicate that 1.000 people were interviewed. Did you personally interview 1.000 people?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were a team of ten people. So it means that about 100 I interviewed myself, but at the end I looked over all the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt here, with permission of my Lord. The question is, there are some leading things coming in and I think this -- I would respectfully say that they may be for instance saying that is it your first-hand knowledge? Saying that: Did you witness it? No, no, he ought to say it himself. This is actually leading the witness. That's what I respectfully wish to point out. And secondly, I would say that referring to paragraphs without their contents being brought here will at least create some problems for the readers later on because I would respectfully say that it will not be a self-contained examination-in-chief, if you kindly can look into this. I'm grateful, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, there is a concern among the Judges here that it's not clear what parts of the transcript this relates to. And just to try to avoid going over it all again and for the sake of clarification, can I ask you whether the first series of questions about the six killings related to page 6, down to where before the last six lines there is a dotted line?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It begins with the paragraph that reads: "From my investigation I have witnesses say ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And second -- the questions you then asked which were about events -- subsequent events related to the part of the statement on pages 6 and 7 in the English, between the two sets of dotted lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. It began on page 7 underneath the first dotted line with the paragraph: "In my position with the council interviewed more than 1.000 people ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's -- what paragraph number do you give that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's paragraph 32, and it begins: "In my position with the CHHRF ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and it carries over to middle of page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, are you -- have you finished your questions on the source --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- of the information? Well, I, for one, find it unhelpful to hear a witness say: I saw some of these myself, I went to the scene, and the rest of them I heard about it. Are we not going to hear what he actually saw for himself? I mean, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it's far more persuasive for any Bench to hear evidence from a witness about what he actually saw himself. Now, it's not for us to direct you. I'll ask -- I'll start asking the questions myself if you're not going down that road. It's up to you; you don't have to. But I certainly want to find out what this witness can actually tell us from his own personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think my colleagues agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday he testified about some things that he had witnessed himself. And in my understanding that was the extent of what he had witnessed himself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've asked a question just now about whether he actually saw certain things himself. I don't know if you expected an answer to be: Well, all of this I heard from others, or not. But you got the answer: Some of it I saw myself because I visited the sites. Now, I at the moment don't know what incidents he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can follow up on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I don't know if you have your statement in front of you, but in connection with the incidents described in paragraphs 34, beginning on page 7 of the English beneath the dotted line you describe killings throughout the municipality. Did you -- did you personally witness any of those killings that are described, beginning on what's in your --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I see them with my own eyes? Yes, in the -- in my own neighbourhood. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court which killing or killings you yourself witnessed.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 50 metres away from my place I saw being killed two brothers, two brothers were killed, at a restaurant nearby, that's 50 metres away from my home. Their surname is Huma, Huma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that specifically mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't -- I haven't put them in my statement, but you are asking me about details and I'm saying them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I find this -- I find this difficult ever since I came to this Tribunal to see these statements which contain all these generalised pieces of information about widespread -- apparently widespread conduct. And then when you do a little probing you discover that what the witness has actually seen that really matters isn't in the statement. How do investigators get these statements into this sort of condition?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I wasn't present at the time that these statements were being taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's very, very unsatisfactory for a Court trying to do this -- a job of this importance to find that statements are being compiled in what looks like a rather unsatisfactory way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's unsatisfactory to the Prosecutor as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, any other killings that you yourself witnessed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ali Beqe Rama, I was just reminded of his name. It's Florenc Sulejmani and the others who were from the village. And all these details have been deposited here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Has that been described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were to include this in my statement, it would be at least a hundred pages. This is very brief, this statement in front of you. With the data that I possess at the centre, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider this statement as very poor in terms of data included.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that was not in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Direct my attention to what the witness told us yesterday he had seen personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know he described when he was in his house, he described seeing paramilitaries burning houses in his neighbourhood. In his statement it's referred to as he saw them throwing cans of petrol and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was on page 7 of the English, Your Honour, the third paragraph down from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just allow us to confer for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you've indicated to us that you find the statement unsatisfactory. Are you saying that you have given to the Prosecution much more material than is reflected in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very little here I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But are you saying that you have told the Prosecution much more? Or are you simply saying that you have got much more to tell which you have not told the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many other things which I haven't yet told the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I, for one, find this a very difficult situation to deal with, Mr. Hannis. You're in the middle of the evidence of the witness and what, on the face of it, needs to be done is for him to be properly interviewed but we're past that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think for the moment all I can do is leave you to continue to examine the witness as you think appropriate. Bearing in mind what is always going to be the approach of this Bench that uppermost in the information we want to hear is what witnesses have actually seen for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with that I want to ask a question, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, about the two killings that you indicated you were -- you had personally witnessed. Did you actually see the killings occur?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was after a few hours that I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may ask a question at this point. Which two killings are being referred to? Because there was a reference to two brothers, but there's also an Ali Beqe Rama and Florenc Sulejmani. Which two killings specifically are being referred to? Could the Trial Chamber please hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I may have gotten the number wrong, but I meant whichever killings he had just told us he had personally seen. I wanted to inquire whether of all of those he actually witnessed the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we don't even know that they're shooting. At the moment this examination is a mess, Mr. Hannis, and really what I'm going to do is adjourn, I think, briefly to allow you to compose yourself and think about how you're going to approach the rest of the examination of this witness and hopefully some constructive approach that will produce from him orderly information about what he saw can be devised. So we'll adjourn for 15 minutes until 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in connection with the a thousand interviews that you indicated were conducted by yourself and a team, who were those thousand people that were interviewed? Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team for the human rights centre, and six members were lawyers who -- who worked in courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, my question referred to the interviewees, the people that you talked to. Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were citizens who had suffered from the violence that was exercised by those forces, and they were all from our municipality, with the exception of one interviewee from Klina, the municipality of Peja, who was a witness to the killing of about 100 people in the village Kralan of Gjakova. The crime occurred in our commune, in our municipality, but I conducted the interview in Klina, in his village. He managed to survive. He had wounds in his body, he had three bullets in his body. And he testified about his friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were those -- I'm sorry. Did you want to finish?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those 1.000 interviews, were those the sources of your information for reporting the incidents that are in your statement, other than the specific things you told us that you personally witnessed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I heard your answer, but -- oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in this order: Counsel for Lukic, Lazarevic, Pavkovic, Milutinovic, Sainovic, and Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. My name is Branko Lukic and together with Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic I appear on behalf of General Lukic before this Tribunal. I wanted to go through your statement the same way my colleague, my learned friend did to try and clarify some things. Mr. Haxhibeqiri, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the transcript reflect both words the witness used to determine his ethnicity? The witness said he was Albanian and Siptar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "Albanian" in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said in Albanian as regards your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are awaiting the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I heard it. I'm surprised you didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're switching between Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. Because of this problem that interpreters have since they have to switch back and forth between two different channels. Could you please repeat your ethnicity once more in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in Albanian what is the word for "Albanian"? What is the Albanian word for "I am Albanian"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the transcript reflect the Albanian word uttered by the witness, since the English translation is somewhat confusing. I can clarify further, but nevertheless we would like to have the transcript reflect the exact word in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, the point -- the point that you're making, Mr. Lukic, appears to be that the word being used by the witness to describe his ethnicity is "Shqiptar." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the Prosecution alleged that it's a derogatory term that Serbs used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But does that answer -- the fact that it's now in the transcript satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Well, carry on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks a lot. [Interpretation] If I may have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I have in front of me your statement dated the 28th of August, 2001. This is P2235. Would you like to be able to see that statement in front of you on the screen? You have the paper copy? On page 2 of the B/C/S, paragraph 4; and page 2 in the English, paragraph 4; page 2 in the Albanian, paragraph 3, there you mention the last real census being carried out in 1981. Can you tell us why there was no census carried out in Kosovo in 1991?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question shouldn't be posed to me. I do not work in statistics, and I'm not part of the body dealing with the census. You know better that during that period you should have carried out that census but you were dealing with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, that that census was not carried out in Kosovo because the Albanians of Kosovo boycotted it?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They never boycotted a census, the Albanians. This figure here is internal, 120.000. You did not allow for the census to take place because you feared that the Albanians would be in great -- far greater numbers than the Serbs. You feared to conduct a census.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, is your testimony here today that Serbia did not make it possible for the Albanians to participate in the census in 1991, which is something Serbia had certainly done throughout its territory?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they didn't do it in Kosova. Officially there is no other statistics recognised other than the ones going back to 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, I would like you to comment on a fact and to say whether it's true or not. In 1991 census was carried out throughout the former Yugoslavia at the federal level, and therefore it wasn't carried out only in Serbia. The only place for which there is no data is Kosovo. Is that correct or incorrect in your view?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accurate. It's true that in Kosova they did not conduct a census. This fact should be known by these people, why the census was not conducted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question to you is the following. In your view, did the Yugoslav authorities try to conduct a census in the territory of Kosovo or not? Did they want to do that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't think it's of importance, this one. If they wanted to do that, they could have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll move on to a different topic, since it is quite clear that you do not wish to provide a clear answer to this. In your statement -- in the B/C/S, page 2, paragraph 5; in the English, page 2, paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, are you intending to put to the witness some specific information about the efforts that were made to carry out the census? If your point is that there was a genuine effort to make -- to carry this out and it was a boycott that prevented it. I mean, that would be strange. It could at least count the people who weren't Albanian. Now, are you saying there was a genuine effort and that there is some effort to show that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll probably bring a demographer in front of this Chamber, so it will be solved at that time. And you will be assured, and I'm sure that you would be assured, that all possible efforts have been made for this census to be successful in Kosovo, as it was successful in any other part of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go back to your statement, sir. Page 2 in the B/C/S, paragraph 5; page 2 in the English, paragraph 5; page 2 in the Albanian, paragraph 4. There you state that as of 1998, the rights of Albanians were systematically undermined. I want to put official data before you pertaining to 1990. In Kosovo there were 22 scientific establishment or facilities with over 1200 employees, among which 213 doctors and 160 masters of sciences, predominantly Albanians. Before the Second World War, not a single Albanian in Kosovo and Metohija held a scientific title --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire what the official data is that counsel is asking this question from. Do we have a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My intention is to ask the witness first and if he says if he's aware of it or he doesn't know or he knows about it, we'll see what his answer is. And I can give you the source from which we collected this data, and it's the book -- maybe it's better for the English translators to translate this title. It says: [Interpretation] "Grabbing of Kosovo and Metohija" by Dragan Milosavljevic, page 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the way the question was phrased was you were putting official data, and Mr. Hannis's question is: What is the official data document. And now you tell us it's a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably from that book we collected it this night, Your Honour. So probably from that book it's visible which source was used during the writing of this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does the book show the source?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can skip this question and come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know, this -- the whole conduct of this examination is becoming more and more chaotic. It's extremely disappointing to be sitting here in court listening to the way in which this evidence is being presented. I've made that comment for the last time today. Please carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I took part in this chaos, but we'll try to improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, on page 2 in the B/C/S, paragraph 6; on page 2 of the English, paragraph 6; and on the second page in the Albanian, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You state the only way to retain your job was to accept the conditions imposed by Serbia. Few Albanians could do this, and they suffered the consequences. Could you please be more specific? What conditions exactly were imposed by Serbia that the Albanians could not accept?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to answer to your previous question. You were talking about some data. In the file the figures refer to 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He has moved on to another question. If Mr. Lukic wishes to return to that question, he will. Please deal with the one he is now asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is: What were the conditions imposed by Serbia that Albanians found it difficult to accept, which meant that they could not continue in their employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted a statement of fidelity to be signed by Albanians that they accepted Serbia as their own state. And the Albanians -- the Albanians could not accept a state who destroyed their parliament by tanks. We could not accept the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us what year that was?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1988/1989 when the autonomy was quashed, when the Albanians, as a result of the persecution, they were forced to leave Kosova. And that's the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is your testimony here that from 1988 and 1989 you no longer consented to staying within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- boycotted that, yes. And I said although there was a boycott -- in fact, you boycotted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To backtrack a little, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, is it correct that the boycott resulted in the Albanians refusing to be a part of the census in 1991?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians were not part of the census, and I'm not aware of a census having taken place, and the reasons -- you know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know what the reasons were, but I'm not the one testifying. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then why do you ask me? I'm not responsible. I only know that there was no census in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, about the relationship between the declaration of fidelity and employment. What was the link between the declaration of fidelity and whether or not you would keep your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meant that asked us whether we recognised Serbia as a state and the violent organs of that state. Of course the Albanians couldn't accept that; therefore, they failed to sign the document. For this reason, they were dismissed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who dismissed them? Their employers dismissed them from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they dismissed all Albanians, and they replaced them with Serbian personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you also said that people who did not sign the declaration could no longer remain within Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They were dismissed from the place of work I meant, and that job was taken by a Serb or a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Was this -- was this dismissal en masse? Was this dismissal en masse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll adjourn as normal until 10.00 -- sorry, until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in 1989/1990, in the early 1990s, did Serbs move into the Djakovica region en masse? Did something like that happen?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any information to that effect. I have never mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that Albanians were losing their jobs, large numbers of Albanians were losing their jobs, and that there were only 2 per cent of Serbs living in the municipality and that the Serbs replaced the Albanians. Is it your testimony today that out of the 2 per cent of the population all the people constituting 98 per cent of the population who were dismissed were replaced by those 2 per cent?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. I think that speaks for itself. Your statement, page 2 in B/C/S, paragraph 7; in the English, it's page 2, paragraph 7; and the Albanian version, page 2, paragraph 5. You talk about how the Albanians did not have access to education. Could you please tell me whether anyone in Kosovo was rejected or not allowed to enroll in school because they happened to be Albanian.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you can tell me about any period.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 when the schools were closed down, when tanks were lined up in front of schools, when hundreds and thousands of Albanians were sacked from their jobs, we set up a parallel system of education, as we described it. We educated our kids in cellars, in mosques and churches, in houses, outside the institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I wanted to ask you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. Is it true that the fact that Albanian children did not attend Serbian schools was not a consequence of segregation by the Serbian state but of a boycott by the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely due to segregation that that happened. You closed down the schools for the Albanians. There were no benches for Albanian children to sit, because when they went to school they saw tanks in front of schools or they saw policemen at the entrance to the schools or to the work-places. The only criterion to be persecuted, to be killed, to be deprived of all rights was to be Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to other rights, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. I'm now asking you about the schooling. You didn't respond. Was any Albanian child not permitted to enroll in a state school because they were an Albanian boy or girl?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that -- it's not a question of enrolment. I am saying that you closed the schools to the Albanian children. You are making it appear as if it was a paradise and that the Albanian children refused to take part in it. This is absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "you," are you thinking of us Canadians? I happen to be Canadian.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand that you are Canadian. I am talking of the current regime at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "you," you are addressing me.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are a synonym of Serbia because you are upholding its colours. This is the way I see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, let me explain something to you about the system that operates here. In the case of each of the accused, they're represented by counsel. These men are each doing a professional job as lawyers. They have no personal interest in the case. The people with a personal interest are the six accused at the far side of the courtroom, and it's wrong in that situation to direct comments of a personal nature towards any of the counsel involved. And indeed, when they ask questions which appear to be taking the side of the accused, they are simply doing the job that they are paid to do. I know that the system is not one with which you are familiar because you come from a country where an entirely different system operates. There's much debate about which is the better, but for good or ill, the system that applies in this Tribunal is one which requires questions of a particular nature, putting the case of the Defence to be put to the witnesses. So please don't view the questions as being put to you on a personal basis either, because we are all anxious to hear as much as we can about your personal knowledge of circumstances that prevailed approximate, particularly in late 1998 and the first half of 1999. On this particular question of education, what's being asked of you is a question that you feel can't be answered in a simple, straightforward way because you're looking at a very big picture. But counsel is asking you to address a particular small issue in relation to that big picture, which is this: If you were Albanian and you wanted your child to go to school, and that is a school provided by the state, would you be able to do that, to take that child along and introduce the child into that state school? Was that still possible after the changes that you claim were made to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already explained that the schools were closed. The tanks were deployed in front of schools. Schools were not functioning at that time in Kosova. I am -- take the courage to speak of Kosova, even though I'm here to speak only for my own municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that the children of Serbs living in Gjakova were not able to go to school either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had their own schools. They continued their lessons normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was there any reason why an Albanian child could not go to one of these schools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not allowed to continue their education. They were driven out of schools. I already said, just because they were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And until this happened, is it your evidence that there were separate schools for Serb children and for Albanian children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is only one Serbian school in our municipality, and in that school went both, Serb and Albanian children, because this is a small town. It has a small number of Serbs and Montenegrins. There were very few classes in Serbian languages taught. There is only one school, primary school, by the name of Emin Duraku. The same applies to the high school, or the gymnasium as we call it. There were few Serb classes taught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did each of the schools you've just mentioned remain open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm talking of Serbian school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph you say: "We organised a parallel educational system for the Albanian children. This was not official." Is it your testimony that all the Albanian children began to attend these schools that you set up?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That question was phrased to the witness: The schools you set up, which I would read him personally. I assume based on our conversation before he means Albanians set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's how I would read it, I think, but perhaps Mr. Lukic would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement that I am reading it states: "We set up a parallel education system for Albanian children." [In English] "We had set up a parallel education system for Albanian children. This was not official." So that's why I asked "you." Anyways -- [Interpretation] In any case, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, at the time when all the children started to go to the schools organised by the Albanians as a parallel educational system, was it normal that all the schools that had been opened before that were closed because they no longer had any pupils to attend these schools?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was not normal because the state was not normal either. They were called schools, as I said, but the lessons were given in cellars, in religious facilities, wherever we could find a place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's a fact that the Albanian children did not go to school, not because Serbian state or the SFRY state did not allow them to do that, but because their parents did not permit them to attend those schools. It was part of the Albanian boycott.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained the reasons for the boycott. I said that a state that closes down parliament through tanks, closes down schools, how can people trust that state? You might call it a boycott, but when children went to schools, or to this school, and found the tanks in front of it, how could the children enter the school I may ask you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the period when the tanks were in front of the schools and how long they remained there? Could you please explain this a little bit more, and which schools were these, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of all primary and high schools. And the period that the tanks were there began in the 1990s. For ten years on end, Albanians didn't have access to the school benches.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is your testimony today that for ten years there was a tank in front of each school?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying that. That the beginning, the first year, it was a signal for them not to go to those schools, to tell the Albanians that: There is no education for you. And if some Albanian student or pupil was caught with books on him or her, he or she was beaten and arrested. And it was a very hard time indeed for those students.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this happened in the late 1980s and early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was during the time that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the abolition [realtime transcript read in error "evolution"] of the autonomy of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So already as of 1989 then?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see the transcript says "evolution." It should be in fact the revocation or -- I think -- well, perhaps in fact on this occasion he said abolition, but it certainly wasn't evolution of the autonomy of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talked about the measures imposed by the Serbian state on Albanians, there's a paragraph on -- in the Albanian version page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- You say that a small number of Albanians were able to -- I apologise. I will start again with the pages because I see that it is wrong in the transcript. This is English version, page 2, paragraph 6; Albanian version, page 2, paragraph 4; and the last sentence in that paragraph says, or you say: "A small number of Albanians were able to accept the conditions imposed by Serbia, and this is why they suffered the consequences." What happened to these few Albanians who did accept to work in the state organs?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the sixth paragraph. In the health sector, they didn't ask the employees to sign this statements of fidelity or loyalty. The Serbs took only the leading positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because of the difference in the way the paragraphs break and the different translations, the question that Mr. Lukic asked actually refers to I think what's numbered as paragraph 4 in the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to confess that I do not understand how the paragraphs can have different -- can be different in different languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a structure that is artificially imposed by the writer on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the different translators did not put paragraph breaks in the same place, so an Albanian version may have 100 paragraphs for the total story; the Serbian version may have 90; and the English version may have 110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that disturbs me because translation should be what it says it is. It should translate word for word what's written and it should translate paragraph for paragraph what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does -- I agree with you, but it didn't happen that way. And sometimes it happens because the translations are done -- sometimes the word formatting is left justified, so there's no indentation at the beginning of the paragraph, and at the bottom of the page the sentence runs completely to the end, the top of the page starts left justified and you don't know if it's a new paragraph or a continuation of the paragraph from the preceding page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it does mean that the paragraphs should have the same numbers. I mean, I find that incomprehensible that it should be paragraph 4 on this the first statement -- page of the witness's statement, it should be paragraph 4 in Albanian and paragraph 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you looked at them side by side I think you would see how it happens that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I shall look at them side by side. If they can be brought up on e-court side by side, let's see why this happens. We're looking at the first -- not the attestation. We want to see the first material page of the statement that's headed with the words "witness statement." It's not the page that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's easiest, I can hand you up hard copies of the English and the Albanian. The first pages ERN in English K0208732, Albanian K0216541, and you can see what happens. Paragraph 4 in the Albanian is divided into two paragraphs in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see -- can you explain, though, why that should be? I just do not understand this, Mr. Hannis. It must be me, but it seems to me basic common sense that if you have a paragraph in English you have a paragraph in Albanian. For example, the second paragraph in English is one line. What's the difficulty about providing that in identical form in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Albanian -- that one line was run together with the preceding paragraph to make one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I was not the translator or the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's not going to take us anywhere. But this is -- it just seems so ridiculous that a translation doesn't replicate the paragraphs, and it makes me wonder if it's accurate. Your immediate reaction to a situation like that is: Does this need to be double-checked? Anyway, I've now lost the thread of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can repeat it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think the difficulty was you were going to have to explain which paragraph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. We are really trying to lessen the confusion, but I don't know how helpful we can be with these kind of paragraphs. But anyways, I was referring to a paragraph in B/C/S page 2, paragraph 6; in English page 2, paragraph 6; and in Albanian page 2, paragraph 4, the last sentence. [Interpretation] I asked the witness: What were the consequences suffered by Albanians who, according to this witness, were few in number, those Albanians who accepted the conditions imposed by the state of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These Albanians, they were loyal collaborators to the regime. They had their own association set up. They were part of the parapolice structures. When the secretariat for internal affairs was closed for the Albanians, the -- they had recruited these committed people who, as I said, were very few in number. They were at the service of the then-state. They were ignored by the Albanian majority because they did not represent the will of the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the fact that they were ignored the only consequence they suffered? You were engaged in human rights work, so did you investigate what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be ignored by the whole society is not an easy thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your investigations connected to the protection of human rights, did you come across situations where such people were killed although they were Albanians, killed by other Albanians because they were working for the state of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. They have been part of every crime within our municipality. They have committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is evidence showing that they committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. Is it your testimony today that in the course of your work, which consisted in investigating human rights violations, you never came across an incident where an Albanian was killed because he was working for the state of Serbia? Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question once more. I did not understand that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that in the course of your investigative work dealing with human rights violations you never encountered a situation in which an Albanian was killed by other Albanians because he was working for the state of Serbia? Mr. Haxhibeqiri, do you find something amusing?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got any case registered in which an Albanian has killed an Albanian because the belligerent part was not the Albanians, it was the Serbs. The war that took place was between the Albanians and the Serbs, not among the Albanians, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. Thank you for giving me this information which shows the extent of your work and the work of your organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also important to remember that that was work from 1995 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to page 3 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 4; page 3, paragraph 2 of the English version; and page 3, paragraph 1 of the Albanian version. Here you again refer to Albanians who agree to work for the state of Serbia. As far as I can see, you put them very low down on the scale of human values. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because these creatures who loyally served the then-system ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you have this kind of opinion about Albanians cooperating with the Serbs, what is your opinion of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Albanians who were sold off and they were upholding the colours of the Serbs against the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Is it correct that your opinion of the Serbs is even worse than your opinion of Albanians collaborating with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not want to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am afraid you'll have to, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, because that is my question and you will have to answer it.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, when I talk about Serbs I talk about the regime there. I'm not commenting about the Serbian people. I do not blame the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a question, Mr. -- with the permission of my Lord Bonomy. Please tell me 25 -- you said about 25 persons or people were won over or suborned by the regime, as you said. I mean, in what way? 25 per cent should be a good number. Can you please give us some illustration or give us some facts how they were won over, a percentage, and they were being pampered by, according to you, as you allege, the others were discriminated. Could you please give us some illustration, anything that -- which could show that they were being pampered, in what way? Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never mentioned the figure of 25 per cent being pampered, as you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I correct myself. Those who cooperated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They formed an association of about 50 members, and I have deposited the list of their membership. It was 53 members in that association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So it means only 53 persons out of the whole population cooperated and not the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, only them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in the same paragraph you referred to people who married a Serb woman, and they were Albanians. What is your opinion about them?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's normal, but politics changed their role because then they turned to be on the side of their partner and commit -- commit crimes against their own population, like the case of Mushk Jakupi or Musa Ibraj. They held the key to the life or death of each and every Albanian. In order to recruit their own cousin, to bring it into the ranks of the police force, him not agreeing, they killed him in their sitting room, and that was in 1999. And they have been present at the scenes of crime before the war, scenes of many crimes even before the war. Also another cousin of theirs, Bajrami, he was arrested by the same person, Ibraj, Muharrem Ibraj, and was executed in the prison of Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, we may conclude that every Albanian who cooperated with the Serbs was a bad man or woman?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was anatomized, good or bad ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take you back to the previous answer about a person called Mushk Jakupi. In your statement he's described as a double Albanian murderer who was imprisoned. When was he in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know the accurate date, but he was a forest guard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly when was he in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1980s, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why was he in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because -- because he had killed someone. He had killed two people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know these characters personally, but this is what people say in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are -- these are two people, different people, from the cousin that you say he murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's father and son. Muharrem is the son, and Musa is the father, 80 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when did he kill them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I'm not sure, but it was during the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. But you then said that he killed a cousin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was -- it was his son. It was his son who committed the crime, Muharrem Ibraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the crime he committed was to kill a cousin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he killed -- he killed his cousin only because he did not agree to join the local police force of the then-regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is an example of an Albanian killing an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't have said that it was an Albanian from the position of an Albanian killing an Albanian. This man was at the service of Serb politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but he was born an Albanian. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Hannis, am I right in saying that there's no reference to this event in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Sorry. I'm looking at paragraph -- on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see the reference to the double murderer, but I don't see a reference to that particular killing you've just gone through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if an Albanian did not kill another Albanian from the position of an Albanian, from what position did he kill him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question's already been answered --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, B/C/S page 3, paragraph 5; English page 3, paragraph 3; Albanian page 3, paragraph 2. You say: "These people that the Serbs found were not the intellectuals. They used people as I've described." Are you saying that in the institutions of Serbia there was no Albanian intellectual who was working there in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the service of the secretariat for internal affairs. They were kind of part of a parapolice formation who were part of the secretariat of interior, and that was just used by the regime to show that even the police force has Albanians in it. And from 1993 onwards there was not a single Albanian in the police force, with the exception of these artificial creatures who formed this association in 1998/1999. They were mainly coming from the villages, people who had problems, and in order to keep hold of a weapon which they badly wanted to have -- or to have monthly wages, because they were in need of that. So they were forced to do that. They did not willingly do that, but in a way they were forced to do it, using the temptation of the land ownership. But I must say that not all of them served loyally to the regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, these artificial creatures, did they exist in other municipalities as well or was this something that happened in Djakovica only?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only in Gjakova, only in Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention the police, is it your testimony that the policemen working in Kosovo who are Albanians had to sign a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that up until 1993 there were Albanians part of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it your testimony earlier on that Albanian policemen lost their jobs because they did not sign a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk about the policemen; I spoke about other organisations. I did not mention the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we conclude that Albanians who were policemen did not have to sign a loyalty oath but that they left the police under the pressure of Albanian politicians and the Albanian community, which was boycotting the state of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question asked to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can repeat it, yes, if necessary. I'll repeat my question. May we conclude that policemen who were Albanians in Kosovo did not have to sign a loyalty oath in order to keep their jobs?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was enormous pressure exerted on policemen by the Albanian community and the Albanian politicians to leave the police force of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the head of the internal secretariat ended up in prison for six years. I know this one. Sejfullah Sahatcijaj his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you believe it to be important and what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Albanian. I said because up until 1993 there were Albanians who were part of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 3, paragraph 9 of the B/C/S; on page 3, paragraph 7 of the English; as well as the third page, paragraph 6 of the Albanian, you state: The police -- or, rather: "The MUP as of 1991 [as interpreted] were brutally beating, arresting, and imprisoning Albanian citizens in Djakovica. It got worse in 1998, the beatings increased, and almost one-third of the citizens 'went through' the MUP offices." Could we please correct the transcript. The first year is not 1991 but 1981. Therefore, the police or the MUP as of 1981 was brutally beating, arresting, and imprisoning Albanian citizens. At that time it was still the SFRY. Isn't that correct, Mr. Haxhibeqiri?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
