utterances.text: And at that time an Albanian was the head of MUP in Djakovica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time most of the policemen were Albanians. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Almost all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reins of power were controlled by the Serbs; they were at the service of Serbian politics. They were operating on the basis of a dictate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Haxhi Hasani was president of state. It was Sinan Hasani, I'm sorry, I apologise, and he was Albanian. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An Albanian who no longer lives in Kosova. He was one of the loyals of the regime. That's how he managed to go up to that position which he was holding then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was loyal to the former SFRY or to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of the B/C/S, paragraph 2; on page 4 of the English, paragraph 1; as well as page 3 of the Albanian, the last paragraph that spills over on to page 4 you state: "We know of two or three people who died as a consequence of torture, one of them was from the village of Pacaj, his name was Halit Zeqe." Zeqe was probably his father's name. "Alia" --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeqe Alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "He was 48 years old and was killed on the 16th of January, 1999. The other one was from the village of Zhdrell, his name was Mark Malota. He was 44 years old and was killed on the 26th of March, 1999." Where do you state that Mark Malota was killed on the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of March in the courtyard of the house of Nazim Karpuska, together with Nazim and Shanin Gojani, while they were distributing aid brought by Mother Teresa association, they were arrested by the MUP. They were cruelly treated during the whole day until Shanin was released first. In the evening, Nazim Kapuska was also released, and he recounted the hell he went through during the hours he was detained in the secretariat building. He could hardly move when he left that building. He was licking his own blood, walking -- hardly walking. He found shelter from one house to another. The forces went to search him because they didn't want to kill him within the building of the MUP. When they went outside, Nazim through his kinsfolk managed to escape. The police followed him. They searched him, asking him where he went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I interject at this point. The correct reference in the English translation is actually page 3, the last paragraph, and not as stated in the record at page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, did you say that the police followed him and then they searched for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they searched for him in those houses where he went, but this person knew the terrain. He knew that the forces would be after him. They released him on purpose in order to kill him outside the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was healed, but Mark never came out alive from that building. His body was found the next morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a word missing in the transcript. What do you say happened to Nazim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nazim managed to escape, and he is alive to this day, and he is an advisor to the mayor of Gjakova municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, Halit Zeqe Alia was arrested in the town by the MUP police on 16th January, 1999. It was midday, if I am not mistaken. These bodies invited the doctor of the town clinic at 5.00 to certify the death. The doctor was my friend, Pleurat Hadri, who came immediately to me and told me that Halit was brought dead and his body is bruised all over and he is still hot, which meant that they had killed him within the building of the secretariat for internal affairs. The doctor was invited to go to the secretariat building immediately. He went there. He certified that the person was dead. They had threatened him, telling him: Bring him back to life. But the doctor told them that the emergency ambulance doesn't have any equipment for him to help the person; therefore, they should send him to the central hospital. And there they all certified the death and he was sent to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to know of this incident?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the doctor is a very close friend of mine. He came up to me immediately, and -- after that and told me about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards the death of Halit Alia and Mark Malota, how did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness who saw him in front of his door killed with a bullet in his head, they -- he told me when they came out in the morning they found the dead body in front of the door in one of the city's neighbourhoods. Mark is from Zhdrell village and he was staying at Nazim Kapuska's house when he was arrested because in his courtyard the Mother Teresa association had its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, I am now completely confused and need to have clarification. Have I wrongly understood Mark Malota to have never emerged from the police office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said he was found dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it to him you refer when you say "they found the dead body in front of the door in one of the city's neighbourhoods"? Is that the person --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking of Mark Malota. He was deputy chairman of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just a little --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the party for democratic league.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, a little earlier when you were telling us about him and Nazim Kapuska you told us that Nazim escaped but that Mark Malota did not come out of the police office alive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he wasn't alive -- he didn't come out alive. He was found dead the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, did you know that on the 26th of March, 1999, in an air-raid carried out by NATO planes next to the Devet Jugovice barracks, Mark Malota was killed as well as Marina Shpeltin [phoen], Vula Hajdar [phoen] and Vula Mahkmut [phoen], and all this you were saying to us is incorrect. What you said about Mark Malota, that is untrue. An onsite investigation was carried out, there are photographs in existence, and we will seek to admit those before this Tribunal and the type of injuries was established as well.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said, they were killed on the 27th of March in Blloku i Ri neighbourhood, the persons you mentioned by name, by the last name of Vula, not in the vicinity of the barracks that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The onsite investigation was carried out by a local magistrate in Djakovica by the name of Cindrag Kemal [phoen], an investigative judge. What was his nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not for you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, to ask questions. You should answer the questions that are put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was Cindrag Kemal's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is this person? I have never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was the then-investigative judge with the local court in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single institution existed in Gjakova. How can you ask me when I was in hiding? I was hiding in a pot-hole by the size of 140 to 120 for four days. I don't know what happened in the city. What trial are you talking about? There was no trial in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not state that there was a trial, but there was an onsite investigation carried out by an investigative judge when the four people were killed during a NATO air-raid.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please mention their names again. You said during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of March, 1999, during an air-raid by NATO planes --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, on the 27th. I was in that neighbourhood. At 5.00 in the morning, a punitive expedition arrived. At 12.00, auto -- cars and Pinzgauers arrived and at 5.00 they torched more than ten houses. This happened on the 27th of March, and 11 persons were arrested, seven persons were killed. Among them are the names that you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not -- in this case, I was not in the pot-hole. I saw everything from the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You stated that as a reply to my question which wasn't recorded in the transcript. A moment ago you said you were in a pot-hole hiding and that you couldn't see anything and you asked me why I was asking these questions. And now you're trying to explain that you were not in that pot-hole and that you actually saw it all. What is correct of these two --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two hours I stayed in that hole, in that pot-hole, and we were eight persons hiding there in that small hole when killings and the torches started. After two hours, when the hunting ended, we came out of that hole and saw the burning houses, and we learned about the persons who were arrested and the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't compare the versions now, but in your statement and in today's transcript you stated that you spent four days in that hole instead of only two hours. Three minutes ago you said you spent four days in that hole. Now you're stating it was two hours. Which of the two is correct? You must tell me.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time that the crimes were committed, I stayed there for -- we stayed there for two hours. Then after that I went back to the -- in the following days to the pot-hole. As of the 2nd of April until the 4th of April, I remained in that pot-hole.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention that in your statement and you didn't mention that on the 51st page of the transcript. You have changed your story now. Now you are stating it differently, Mr. Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated earlier that I have so much stuff to tell you that even 100 pages wouldn't be enough to recount them. Sure, you'll see a book of 600 pages where you'll see facts about everything that I'm saying. You have killed the persons yourself --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were alone in that hole. Now you said: "There were eight of us," and you can tell me when. When were you alone and when were you with another eight people?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of March, in the morning of that day, I was there along with eight persons. We were altogether eight persons. On the 2nd of April, when they had driven out almost 30.000 people from that neighbourhood, I remained in that pot-hole because I was afraid to come out and cross the border, because being an activist at that time I was afraid that my name would be black-listed. So this is the reason why I remained there hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it still your testimony that Mark Malota was not killed during an air-raid by NATO planes but rather that he was killed in the building of the secretariat for internal affairs in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the beginning of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that Mark Malota was not killed during a NATO air-raid, that he was not killed by a NATO bomb, but rather that he was killed inside the SUP building in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO didn't fire with bullets. He was found dead with a bullet in his head. And in our city only -- we had only one victim inflicted as a result of NATO bombings. He was dead because of the NATO air-strikes, and his last name is Gjoshi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you received such information that he was killed by bullets and not by bombs? What is the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was found dead with a bullet in his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the bodies were exhumated by the ICTY, none of them was found to be dead as a result of NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that this Tribunal forwarded exhumation data to you? I'm really interested to know where you received that information from.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there present during exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you must have been told by someone. You are not an expert to be able to determine how someone was killed.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They provided me with a list of the exhumed persons. I have also the names of the persons who were killed -- I mean, even with what weapons they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, are you saying that the first information you received that Malota was shot through the head came from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which Prosecution, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that the first time you learned that Malota had been shot was as the result of information from the Prosecution here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- can you refer me to the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm saying that I learned of his death on the very day that his body was found, because my house is very -- within short distance from that place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just hold on. The reason for me asking this, Mr. Hannis is the answer: When the bodies were exhumed by the ICTY, none of them as found to be dead as a result of NATO bombing." And that's a direct answer to the question: What is the source of your information? And I'm asking if the first he heard that Malota was shot through the head was information from this Tribunal. Now, is that the first time you learned that he had been shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I went to the -- I went to the place -- to the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was looking -- I didn't go exactly there, but I was a side-looker, onsite-looker, and then I was waiting for the findings of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what did you see at the scene of Malota's death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see anything there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I ask you again: Was the first time you learned that he had been shot when this Tribunal told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who saw him with his own eyes told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His last name is Lleshi. He was -- the body was found before the door of this person's house. His last name is Lleshi. He lives near Ura e Tobakeve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic, you referred to having material which was compiled in a -- an onsite investigation, and you referred to photographs --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but it's not translated yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you've got a photograph of a body that shows it doesn't have a bullet in the head --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've just been informed, Your Honour, that it might be in the system, because the other team was more diligent than us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if there's something to show the identity of this person and any evidence of his death that could be put to the witness if you wish to contradict his account --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- on that basis. And we'll now adjourn and resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we start, I'd like some clarification, Your Honours and Mr. Lukic, about the character we were talking about. It's true, as Mr. Lukic was saying, there was no bullet. When I went during the break, I was reminded. So I do apologise. It's the -- another character, Urim Rexha, who was killed on the same date. He was shot in the head, and during the exhumation he was found that he was shot -- it was found that he was shot. And there was a confusion of persons. He was the founder of the LDK in the region, Urim Rexha. He was shot in his own home; whereas Mark Malota, he was found but without bullets in his body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Just one question arising from it. Do you have any information about the cause of his death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I -- I only know that nobody saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you also saying then that the information you gave about where he was found is wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Everything else is -- everything else is accurate, but for the detail that the bullet was in somebody else's head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since this witness has no knowledge about the death of Mr. Malota, I wouldn't pursue this issue any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He explained that -- what he said before and he explained what he thinks now and we think that it's self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need for us to waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in your statement, page 4 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 2; and page 4, paragraph 1 in English; page 3 in Albanian, the last paragraph, and the first paragraph on page 4. After we mentioned these people, you say with reference to Novak Pitulic, Momcilo Stanojevic, and the existence of the local Crisis Staff, and you also mention the name of Dragutin Prentic, a journalist, you say that Momcilo Stanojevic was the author of many of the crimes that were committed around town. Could you please clarify the role of this Crisis Staff, please.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the municipality then, and of course he was a collaborator, a -- the most committed collaborator at the time. In my opinion, he was the architect of many crimes carried out in town. He was assisted of course by some others like Dragutin Prentic, a journalist with Jedinstvo newspaper, who has been seen -- was seen in Meja recording crimes there. And many witnesses testified that they have seen him in Meja filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Haxhibeqiri, what I'd like to know is what kind of powers and competences this Crisis Staff had, whether it controlled life in the town; and if so, in what way.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The powers of the Crisis Staff should be known by those who founded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, we don't know the powers of the Crisis Staff. The only way we can obtain information as Judges to make a decision in this case is from the answers given by witnesses to the questions that are posed. So please answer the question that counsel has asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I have a document with me at the hotel which explains what I have said here on the statement. On the 31st of April of 1999, he was elected as the chairman of the Crisis Staff, and it's Momcilo Stanojevic. I can only bring here a list of the persons who at the time have been operating in Gjakova and the decisions that they have taken. The document that I have has been signed by General Milos Djokan [as interpreted]. There you can find the names of all those who organised life in the municipality during the war, and they are the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give again the name of the general you say signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos Djosan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you now answer the question that was actually asked of you or tell me that you are not in a position to, one or the other. You were asked what were the powers of the Crisis Staff? In other words, what did it do? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document will explain everything, and I can bring that document to you. And it's written in the original Serbo-Croat language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your position on that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Presently we don't have any before we see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want the document to be brought here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have nothing against to see the document. Why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I could -- if I may, Your Honour. I might ask two or more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, in your view de facto could this Crisis Staff command units of the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, were they in control? Did they have control over the police and over Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. We'll move on to the next part of your statement. Let's now move on to page 5, paragraph 5 in B/C/S; page 5, paragraph 4 in English; and page 5, paragraph 2 in Albanian. You say that before shelling the police and the army would go to the villages looking for the KLA. They asked villagers if they had seen the KLA. They would accuse the whole village of supporting the KLA. They constantly told the people: Go to Albania, otherwise we will kill and burn you all. Then these mixed forces would burn or shell the villages, forcing the people from their houses. This continued during the NATO bombing. What you state here refers to the period before the NATO bombing, is that correct, and then it continues during the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Not only during the 78-day period of the bombing, but also from March and April 1998 villages were being shelled, they were burned, people were forced out of their homes, and this -- there have been cases when they went back to their homes but they were forced to leave again. Their homes were burned. So during that period, there was a large-scale migration of the population. And during that period the violence against the population has only -- only intensified during the October 1998, after the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement and only after the OSCE mission to Kosova went on the ground. This violence increased to a larger scale. I have recorded more than 50 villages which were destroyed and burned, partially or completely. And this is for the period that I'm talking about. And there are 160 people killed, of which -- of whom I have all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that the situation was the worst while the verification mission was there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the verifiers who were on the ground could confirm what you say? Did you report the incidents that took place on the ground to them?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, continuously. For every crime that took place, they were informed. We've jointly gone out on the ground and we've recorded all the cases of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did representatives of the state go out on the ground together with the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of which state you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The state of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if they tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether representatives of the state went out on to the ground together with you and with the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was out there, I was there only with members of the OSCE mission and nobody else. Of course the OSCE mission was escorted. They couldn't go there on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was it that escorted them, Mr. Haxhibeqiri?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. On page 5, paragraph 6 of the B/C/S version; and page 5, paragraph 5 of the English version; and page 5, paragraph 3 of the Albanian version you talk about the burning down of villages, shelling. And you also mention which parts; south-west of town, Dushkaja, Mahalla, a group of villages north-east of Djakovica. You are in fact speaking about the period when there were intense fights between the KLA, the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about fighting between the Yugoslav army and MUP? Is there a mistake there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On one side and then the KLA on the other.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These villages were shelled from the hill of Cabrat, which is near Gjakova. That's the hill of the chestnut trees in Decan and the hill of Pllanik, every day in the name of -- allegedly, of the war against the KLA. Every day and every night it -- shells were coming on those -- on those villages. The citizens were forced to leave their homes and take shelter in Gjakova, in the town of Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you know in these villages that you mentioned if there were any KLA forces there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go out into the field in those villages at that time?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if that's a complete answer, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. The question is whether you had any knowledge of the presence of any forces, any of the KLA forces in any of the villages. And your statement indicates there are a large number, 85 villages. Now, did you not have any knowledge of any KLA forces in that area at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They stayed in the peri-urban area. Nobody saw them, but I suppose there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time policemen and soldiers were getting killed, members of the Army of Yugoslavia and MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because we didn't have any information on -- as an organisation I'm saying, on the murder or killing of the Serbs. They were -- they did not allow us to have information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there a village called Shishman Boges in the municipality of Djakovica? And I apologise if I mispronounce the name.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 30th of March, 1999 members of the KLA carried out an attack against members of the police and Radovan Jorgin [phoen] was killed and Ermin Bogucanin was seriously wounded in that attack. The last one is a Muslim as well as a person called Zoran Mosorinski. Are you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is the first time for me to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 1st of April, 1999, members of the KLA carried out an attack at Misko Rajevic, member of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the village of Zdrelo in Djakovica on the night between the 1st and 2nd of April, 1999, members of the KLA carried out an armed attack on the house of Lushaj Tome, an Albanian from the village of Zdrelo?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that in the midnight of the 1st and 2nd April of 1999 about 100 people got killed; or, to be more precise, 80-some, I can't remember. Just a moment, maybe it will come to my mind. 75 persons, Albanians, they were civilians. They were killed. Of them, 11 were children. The remainder were old men and women, young women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the municipality of Djakovica, after the 24th of March, 1999, was constantly in a state of war being conducted between the KLA and the Yugoslav forces and that it was also being bombed by NATO at that same time?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO was bombarding the military bases deployed in Cabrat hill and Emin Duraku barracks, situated south of Gjakova town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many times were those targets hit; do you know?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many -- countless times, until they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Djakovica was bombed 265 times in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the bombs -- I think the merit for the bombs goes to you, because it was you who brought them and you were in a position to stop them and you did that. When the time came, you signed the Kumanova Agreement; a military-political agreement that was. You allowed them yourselves. I think the merit goes to you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you think that I have any contribution or any part in that bombing, but since I cannot testify from here I will continue to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to apologise to you, to address you, but by "you" I mean all this side as -- which for me is an opponent side. But by this I mean mostly the accused who stand behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how intense was the fighting between the KLA and the Serbian forces during the period of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fighting lasted from 7 to the 11th of April. After that date, there was no more fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was the KLA a strong force?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the KLA a well-organised force?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they look like an army at all?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, no, but later on yes, it assumed the form of an army. Because it was spontaneously formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when does this period begin, this later time?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of 1998 and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did members of the KLA wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially no, but later on yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us again when was it, this later, when they began to wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they became more widespread. It was the second half of 1998, if I am not wrong. Because I was not there on the ground to see them, but from the documentaries we watched I came to the conclusion that this was how it happened. It was that when they got uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have information that they were armed people moving around but without uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They did not move around? There were no such people or you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So all your knowledge about the KLA, and this is your testimony today, comes from documentaries, documentary films?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I saw after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out any investigations relating to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigation into what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding violations of human rights committed by members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What violations are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never heard that members of the KLA committed any violations of human rights?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You killed the Albanians. You have violated human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, just to finish with this topic today, that you never heard of any human rights violations or crimes committed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such violations. I haven't seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We'll continue. If there is any need to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the second time -- I refrained previously when you made a comment and -- from interrupting. Please restrain yourself to asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Bear with me, Your Honour, just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, would you kindly tell us what the ethnic composition is of the organisation that you are chairman of, the one that investigated violations of human rights.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who paid your salaries, Mr. Haxhibeqiri?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked on a voluntary basis. We were not paid for that. Only the rent for the office was paid by the centre. Rent, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you earn a living in some other way from 1995 until the end of 2002?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I worked in a shop owned by the Agimi Organisation, but it was burned. And after the war I continued to work for the same organisation but now for payment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us the organisation that you were a chairman of for a certain amount of time. What exactly did you do in your investigations that you carried out? What did they consist of?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We conducted the investigations after the war. The organisation, the ICG group came to the town of Gjakova and they engaged me with my people to work for them for five months to collect data on the crimes committed in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they indicate to you which evidence you were to gather during the five months that you worked for them?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They gave us a questionnaire prepared by them - I may show you copies if you want - with the questions which we were supposed to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the ICG never told you to go and investigate human rights violations committed by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed violations of -- violations committed by KLA because none of the dead persons whose files we have in our office have been committed by the KLA; they've all been committed by the Serb soldiers, militaries, and paramilitaries aided by the local Serbs because they knew the persons, that is, the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. The next question I would like to clarify with you relates to the part of your statement on page 7, paragraph 4 of the B/C/S version; page 6, the last paragraph, the ninth paragraph, of the English version; and page 6, last paragraph of the Albanian version. You say that the son of Mushk Jakupi came and -- to the house where you took shelter in Blloku i Ri, that two policemen came in a blue vehicle, and that one of them was Mushk Jakupi, and that they told you: Leave the house within five minutes. If you do not go, we will throw a hand-grenade. Just for the record, what is Mushk Jakupi by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mushk is a pet name. His name is Musa Ibraj. He is an Albanian, but he was recruited as a local police. He was a loyal policeman, as we described him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He threatened everybody in the house that he would send them off to Albania. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He and another policeman dressed in blue, light blue uniforms, because the uniforms were different. They came in and banged the door open and told us to leave in five minutes, otherwise: You will be dead. We will throw bombs. The bus is waiting for you at the church. All of you should -- must go to Albania. That -- those were their words. And during the day the entire neighbourhood of Blloku i Ri, which numbers about 30.000 inhabitants, had to be emptied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thus, an Albanian is expelling an Albanian to Albania. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that along with him there was another policeman dressed in a light blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the local police that was under the control of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was under anyone's control. Other people know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you mentioned these light blue uniforms you say they were different. Different from what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The regular police used to wear dark blue uniforms; whereas those local police, as we saw them, wore a kind of olive-green-to-brownish colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the earlier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very different from the regular police uniform in colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can understand if it's olive-green or brown it would be, but the initial answer that's been recorded here was that he and another policeman dressed in blue, light blue uniforms, because the uniforms were different. Is that inaccurate, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of them, yes, he was wearing a blue uniform, but not the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the light blue uniform a uniform of? Was that the regular Serb police or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know even the policeman in person. His name was Avramovic. I think his last name was Avramovic. He used to work in the MUP where we registered the car and got the license plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he was wearing a regular police uniform. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wore a police uniform. All of them were -- most of them, to be accurate, were recruited, that is the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next paragraph -- actually, just one second. Page 7, paragraph 6 of the B/C/S version; page 7, paragraph 2 of the English version; 7 -- page 7, paragraph 2 of the Albanian version. That paragraph is just one line in my copy, and it says that four days after -- four days after the time that you were hiding you returned to your house and you stayed until the war was over.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After four days of staying in that manhole, I returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening I left the house when firing stopped. After 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening, I left the house, taking great care and hiding often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People knew that you were in the house?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which people do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's say your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated here that the 30.000 inhabitants of that neighbourhood were driven away. Only the houses who were there which were taken over -- I mean in which lived the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It means that your neighbours were Serbs and they knew you were there?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they knew, I wouldn't be here today. They came there every day during my stay in the manhole. They came and looted the houses. It was the house of Gani Efendiu, whose family was displaced. And behind his house I was there in that manhole, as I told you, and the Serb forces came there every day and they looted the assets of those houses in lorries. They looted the houses of all Albanians in that area. Where I was, near that place was the doctor's clinic. He had all the equipment there, and I saw them taking out all his equipment. All the appliances he had there, they took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The authorities, too, knew you were at that house. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... knew other than the family of the doctor whose members left me there in that manhole when they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in the B/C/S page 9, second paragraph; in the English version, page 8, the eighth paragraph; in the Albanian version, page 8, paragraph 6. There you state: "From the end of April 1992 [as interpreted], two male and two female police officers started to register the Albanians left in the municipality." These police officers, did they come to your doorstep to register you?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't come, because in the area where I lived almost all the neighbourhood was burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your house burnt down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, the English translation has "1999." Is it 1999 or 1992, as was stated, just to be doubly sure?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that my house was partially burned and it was my brothers who managed to put out the flames, and the boys in the neighbourhood who helped out and luckily it was saved. And the same night that it was set alight there was rain which helped to put out the flames. My uncle's house was entirely burned which is metres away from my house. All the bars and restaurants around my place, about 20, were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you discussed the fighting between the 7th and the 11th of May in Djakovica, although this is not part of your statement given to us by the OTP, you described the street fighting in the town of Djakovica itself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the streets there were no fighting. The fighting was in the hill of Cabrat in the west of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said that in the fighting around 100 KLA soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were killed -- I said civilians, more than a hundred civilians. Approximately 106, if I'm not mistaken, more than a hundred houses burned and arrested about 300 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of whom 150 ended up in Serbian prisons as hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, does this appear somewhere in the statement? And in particular the reference to the house being partially burned and then the uncle's house being entirely burned? Is that in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. This part that deals with fightings in between KLA and Serbian forces is not in his statement. If it is, I would like my learned colleague from the other side to enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know, though, that it is in the transcript for yesterday at page 51 -- [In English] Actually, 1078 of the updated version, 1078.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that 150 people out of the 300 that were taken prisoner were kept as hostages. Did you know whether any investigations were carried out against those people as -- so as to check whether they belonged to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because they were in that area where fighting was taking place, they were considered as such. But all these civilians were taken away from their homes or the centre of the city. They were threatened with their lives; if they don't leave their homes, they would be killed. Together with them was a cousin of mine who is a doctor of sciences, and he was together with 146 other people. But because of the shelling and all the fear that the children would not be able to cope and under the threats of the police, the people were forced to go to Albania. In the -- but in the centre of the city towards the Assembly, the children and women were taken away to the factory of Electromotos [phoen], where up to 2.000 people were held and they were held separately from their parents, whereas the rest were sent to the outskirts of Gjakova to a joinery shop where they were maltreated. They were given a slice of bread and a piece of cheese for a period of 24 hours. And that was given only to the kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I needed was the yes you said at the very beginning and the rest is not in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To clarify one thing. The -- you stated a little time ago that the fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces took place during a certain period, and you gave the dates. Can you remind me of these dates, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7th to the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. At one stage April was used, but it is May you are referring to. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, May. I was always talking about May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one question left to conclude this cross-examination, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. This was discussed with you by my learned friend on page 17, line 3. You personally did not see a single murder. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have seen people who were killed, but I haven't witnessed one being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. My learned friends will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haxhibeqiri, my name is Djuro Cepic, attorney-at-law, member of the Defence team representing General Lazarevic. I have a few questions for you. Are you prepared to respond to them to provide your replies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for him, Mr. Cepic. Just carry on and ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would briefly comment on the census data and this was touched upon by my colleague Lukic. You mentioned an approximate figure of inhabitants of Djakovica at that time. As regards Albanians, what was the percentage of the Muslim population and what was the percentage of Catholic population?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We haven't got any details in terms of percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: By approximation do you know what the ratio was in the villages around Djakovica? How many villages were predominantly Muslim and how many were predominantly Catholic? Did you have any precise data as to the numbers of inhabitants then?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no pure villages, religiously pure; they are mixed. Some of them have more Christians, some of them have fewer, but there are no villages with a religiously pure majority. Mainly they are inhabited by Christians. It could be 30 per cent Christians in our municipality. I may be wrong. That includes the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me if I said that there was no precise data as regards the number and percentages of various ethnicities in the total population?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are official figures coming from the Assembly, but I can say about -- about 70, 80 per cent are Albanians in Gjakova. And as for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago you said that only 2 per cent of them were Serbs and over 80 per cent were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. 98 per cent, 98 per cent, sorry. As for Serbs, it can go up to 3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How come you have such precise data, since the last census was in 1981, the last complete census?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the official figures. What can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What official data pertains to 1998 and 1999, Mr. Haxhibeqiri? I have in mind the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For before the war I haven't got any figures because there was no census conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haxhibeqiri. In brief, I'd like to touch upon the issue of education, that is paragraph 7, page 2 of the English transcript; and also paragraph 7 in the B/C/S. There you state that the rights of Albanian children were violated because they were unable to attend school. Can you tell me how many elementary schools were there in the territory of the Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city there were four primary schools and four middle or high schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And in the entire territory of the Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there an answer to that question, the number of schools in the whole municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 20. I'm not sure because I'm not specifically dealing with these issues, but I haven't got accurate figures. You can ask other people who were specialised on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why did you provide your opinion in the statement as regards that issue if you are not the person to be asked that question?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I believe you did understand me, but I will repeat nonetheless. Why did you then provide your opinion in your statement dated the 28th of August, 2001. In the English, that is page 2, paragraph 7. There you state that the right to attend school by Albanian children was violated. I quote: "Many of the people who left were young people to whom education was not available."

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me about the existing schools, as Serb institutions, facilities. You didn't ask me whether teaching was taking place in those schools. Which paragraph is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I don't have the Albanian version --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's paragraph 5 on his Albanian version. And, Your Honour, I guess while I'm up I would object to the form of the question. I think it's somewhat argumentative. He asked him about the number of schools, he said about 20-some, that he was not an expert on that figure. That wouldn't preclude him from necessarily having an opinion about whether Albanian children were denied an opportunity to have an education.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Hannis. I was just waiting to hear what the answer was. Why don't we move on to something productive, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question concerning that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that elementary education in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija as well as in the territory of the entire Republic of Serbia was obligatory?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Did you know that in all those elementary schools, apart from the school of Emin Duraku, where teaching was conducted in both Serbian and Albanian, whereas in all the other schools teaching was conducted in only Albanian?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on to another topic pertaining to health care. This is paragraph 8, page 2 in the B/C/S -- [In English] Line -- actually, paragraph number 7 in English version. [Interpretation] There you state that Albanians could not enjoy health care --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to make a clarification. When talking about the primary schools, it is true that -- that a number of these facilities was used with four shifts, but all the -- as for the payment, it was from the contributions of the population, and that was in an attempt to keep the Albanian education alive. You did not finance the Albanian education. Only the physical premises were there to be used for the children of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son was of that school age at the time. The middle or high schools were closed, and the -- as was the university, the university was closed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who financed that education?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why was then a parallel system in existence as you stated yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness keeps shifting between B/C/S and Albanian and both speakers overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was -- the Albanians were paying for the teachers. There was a council for financing the parallel system, and all the Albanian diaspora were contributing a certain percentage to keep the Albanian education alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you haven't answered my question. Why were the two parallel systems financed then?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about when you say "two systems"? I'm talking about the Albanian system. There was no other system. We were alienated. We were kept away from other systems. For the primary school children only, the premises, the school premises, were made available, only for the primary school kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why do you state then that there were tanks in front of schools?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why did you let your children go to school then, to have to go next to the tanks and above all primary-age children -- primary-school aged children?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no tanks in front of the elementary schools. The tanks were in front of the middle and high schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you state that previously in your statement, the way you are putting it now?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you didn't. You are now coming up with all this information, whereas a while ago you said you knew nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the statement is too deficient when you think of the wealth of information that I possess.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that is a time for a break, if you allow us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We will break now and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have come to the question on health protection on page 2, paragraph 7 of the English version; and on the same page, paragraph 8 of the B/C/S version you said that the Albanians suffered because of the health coverage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even that the health system suffered consequences, but not as bad as those for the education. But there were consequences, because it was a repressive Serbian body who was in charge. They removed the Albanian specialists in the hospital and they installed a Serbian doctor, and they did the same in the ambulance of the city. A Serb doctor was employed there. He was the only one in the clinic. Before there were 24 Albanian specialist doctors. That means that the Albanian specialists were removed, the specialists were removed, and a Serbian doctor was employed instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Something is not clear to me. In your statement of August 28th, 2001, you mention that only two Serbs were doctors in Djakovica; in the capacity of the director or manager of the medical centre and the other person was the administrator of the medical centre. But today you said there were several doctors?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two who were employed in the health bodies. And those 24 specialists who I mentioned earlier, they were all Albanian. And there was this doctor who was employed in the clinic of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I still don't understand your answer. Were there only two doctors in a -- Serb doctors in Djakovica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop for a moment. You're speaking over each other now. I gather you're moving between languages at times, and therefore the question and answers speed up. It's important that you pause after the question before starting the answer so that the interpreters can catch up. Secondly, there isn't an answer on my screen that suggests there was more -- there were more Serb doctors employed. Where has that information come from, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I'm saying is that the witness asserted that there were only two, while in the previous statement he said that there were several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where -- in which previous statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honour, just to stop for a second. I do apologise, but I can't find transcript right now on my screen. So may I continue the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, not on that basis without establishing that there is an answer in which he said that there were several Serb doctors. You can move to something else while it's being checked, if you like. But if you're going to persist on this line, then we need to get it set on a proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 28th of August, page 5, paragraph 8 of the English translation; page 6, paragraph 2 of the B/C/S translation you said that you reported Voice of America, Deutsche Welle, and some other well-known media organisations, that you sent reports to them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of the B/C/S version; or page 4, paragraph 6 of the English version, you say in the last sentence that you reported to the newspapers about what was happening --

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Listen carefully to the question and Mr. Cepic will start it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As I said, page 4, paragraph 6 of the English and page 5, paragraph 1 of the B/C/S translation the witness said in that statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Cabrat hill --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is that the witness is working from an Albanian translation which you're not giving the details of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't speak Albanian, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nor, I suspect, does Mr. Hannis but he's done the witness the courtesy for identifying for him in his statement where the paragraph is. That's a necessary courtesy that you must observe with a witness who speaks Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If counsel could indicate to me what the first line is of the English, I could direct the witness to the Albanian paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please. "The Serbs had large cannons placed in Podi" -- I'm speaking about that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You're on page 4 of the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph on page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's paragraph 16 in the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please pose the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last two lines there is the sentence by

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I was informed on a daily basis which units were operating. Up to the time that the newspapers were closed down, I reported to the newspapers about these events." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You sent reports to which newspapers?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only newspaper had -- had a changed name, Bujku.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You are asserting then that in that period - and I'm talking about 1998 and 1999 - in Kosovo and Metohija there was only one newspaper?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I were to tell you that in that period there was a considerable number of media that were being published in Kosovo in the Albanian language? I will just mention some of them, such as Koha Ditore, it's a daily; Kosovo Sot, daily; bi-weekly Gazeta Shqiptare Bota e Re magazine; Rilindja, and so on.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read a lot, but I'm not aware. Bujku before was called Rilindja because it was not allowed to be published under that name and it changed into Bujku. As for the others, I'm not aware of them. I haven't seen them. I did not see them, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you are asserting that there was only one newspaper in Albanian that was being published in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware -- as far as I'm aware, there was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis, your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The question now is: You're asserting there was only one newspaper in Albanian that was being published. He's only saying he was only aware of one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or that he had only seen one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Haxhibeqiri, the -- you were given a list of newspapers just now which included Koha Ditore and others. Had you heard -- have you heard of that newspaper -- have you heard of that newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have heard about Koha Ditore, but the others not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the position with that newspaper during the period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, was it being published during the period that you're talking of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This newspaper was published, but it was published under very difficult circumstances, under all sorts of threats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that clear the point for you, Mr. Hannis, or does it just complicate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess it complicates it somewhat. I'm not sure what period of time we're talking about exactly right now either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that I did indicate the period that I was focussing on for purposes of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty about that point is that the paragraph in question doesn't indicate the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We heard today and you confirmed that in your previous sentence that at least two Albanian-language papers were published. You said Bujku and you confirmed about Koha Ditore. Why did you then say in your statement that there was only one weekly that was published? This is on page 3, paragraph 7; and in English it's page 3, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It maybe there is some translation mistake or something like that. Or maybe when I made that statement I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... believe that to be a translation mistake?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. [Interpretation] I would like the registry to open up Exhibit 5D3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhibeqiri, you previously confirmed that you gave several interviews to the foreign media. In front of me I have the part of an interview that you gave and which was published on the official presentation of the state university of New York at Buffalo. Did you cooperate with the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are we talking about? Which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about after the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not had any previous cooperation with the Tribunal, apart from when I gave this witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 3 of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the problem producing this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy, Mr. Cepic? We seem to have technical problems every time we want to use this system.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have got enough copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what language is the copy that you've given the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, because the time was short we only have a copy in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll need to read the part that you want to put to him so that it can be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read line 10 of page 3, I'm going to read it in English. [In English] "We were directly involved, Haxhibeqiri said, citing course of witness statement that his organisation has forwarded to international war crimes investigator in The Hague."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this true?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is, first of all? Is this an interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is your interview published by the LA Times in which you talk about the situation in Kosmet. Did you give this interview at all?

utterances.speaker: FUAT HAXHIBEQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given many interviews, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Cepic, that you wish to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first question is whether he did give this interview, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't given him a date for the interview or a place. I mean, how can he be expected to answer the question? He's got a document in a strange language in front of him. And even when we get to that stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Monday, the 18th of October, 1999. The document was published through the Albanian journalist information network.
